ConnectWise warns of new ScreenConnect flaw without patch

ConnectWise warned of a new unpatched ScreenConnect file transfer vulnerability affecting cloud and on-prem deployments and urged admins to temporarily disable file transfer permissions until a fix is released later this week.
KEY POINTS
  • 01ConnectWise issued temporary mitigation measures for a new ScreenConnect Remote Access vulnerability that it plans to patch later this week.
  • 02The flaw affects file transfer behavior in ScreenConnect Remote Access Support and Access sessions across both cloud and on-premises deployments, and it has not yet received a CVE ID.
  • 03ConnectWise advised administrators to disable the TransferFiles permission, or TransferFilesInSession for legacy versions, for each session group assigned to user roles.
  • 04Shadowserver is tracking nearly 6,000 ScreenConnect instances exposed online, though it is unclear how many are honeypots or have already been secured.
  • 05The article states that ScreenConnect vulnerabilities have often been targeted by financially motivated and state-backed hacking groups, including prior exploitation by ransomware gangs and the Kimsuky North Korean APT group.

ConnectWise has shared temporary mitigation measures for a new ScreenConnect Remote Access vulnerability that it plans to patch later this week. The issue affects file transfer behavior in ScreenConnect Remote Access Support and Access sessions. ConnectWise said the flaw affects both cloud and on-premises deployments, and it has not yet received a CVE ID.

The company advised administrators to log in to the ScreenConnect Administration page, review roles under Administration > Security > Roles, and check session groups with assigned permissions. In the Scoped Permissions window, administrators should deselect the TransferFiles permission, or TransferFilesInSession for legacy versions, for each session group. Shadowserver is tracking nearly 6,000 ScreenConnect instances exposed online, though the article notes it is unclear how many are honeypots or already secured.

ScreenConnect vulnerabilities are often targeted in the wild by financially motivated and state-backed hacking groups. The article cites past exploitation by ransomware gangs and the Kimsuky North Korean APT group, as well as a prior suspected state-sponsored breach involving a high-severity ViewState code injection bug. It also notes that CISA has added three ScreenConnect vulnerabilities to its catalog of actively exploited flaws since February 2024, two of which were also abused in ransomware attacks.

  • The mitigation is permission-based rather than version-based, so administrators can reduce exposure before a software patch is available by removing file transfer rights from affected roles and session groups.
  • The issue is serious enough for ConnectWise to publish interim defensive steps before assigning or referencing a CVE, indicating administrators cannot rely on CVE-based tracking alone for this flaw.
  • Because ScreenConnect is commonly used by MSPs and IT support teams, a flaw in its remote access or file transfer functions can affect organizations beyond a single end customer environment.
  • The article highlights a recurring pattern of ScreenConnect flaws being targeted after disclosure, including multiple vulnerabilities added to CISA’s known exploited catalog since February 2024.

ConnectWise warned about a new problem in its ScreenConnect remote access tool that affects both online and self-hosted versions, and it does not have a permanent fix yet. The company is telling administrators to turn off file transfer permissions for now to help prevent possible misuse. This matters because ScreenConnect is used by IT support teams and managed service providers to access and maintain computers, and similar ScreenConnect problems have previously been used by criminal and government-backed hackers to install harmful software or break into customer systems.

Magento StyleSmuggler zero-day exploited to deploy Linux backdoor

A Magento and Adobe Commerce zero-day dubbed StyleSmuggler is being actively exploited to install a Linux backdoor, including on fully patched systems. Until Adobe releases a fix, admins should consider disabling GraphQL and check for suspicious failed-payment emails, cron jobs, and disguised kworker or fc-cache processes.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A zero-day vulnerability dubbed “StyleSmuggler” affects all versions of Magento and Adobe Commerce and is being exploited to deploy a backdoor.
  • 02Sansec recorded the first exploitation incident on September 4 against a target running the latest security updates.
  • 03The exploit abuses Magento’s template system through PHP code injection to generate a fake “failed-payment” email that triggers code execution.
  • 04Successful exploitation installs a small Rust-based backdoor as a background process, with newer versions disguising it as fc-cache and copying it to ~/.cache/fontconfig/fc-cache.
  • 05Sansec recommends disabling GraphQL as a mitigation until Adobe releases fixes for StyleSmuggler.

A zero-day vulnerability dubbed “StyleSmuggler” affects all versions of Magento and Adobe Commerce and is being exploited in attacks to deploy a backdoor. Sansec recorded the first exploitation incident on September 4 against a target running the latest security updates. Adobe Enterprise Support confirmed it was working on a fix, but did not provide a release timeline.

Magento is an Adobe open-source e-commerce platform installed on more than 160,000 websites, including 14,000 of the top 1 million sites. The exploit observed by Sansec abuses Magento’s template system through PHP code injection to generate a fake “failed-payment” email, which triggers code execution. Successful exploitation installs a small Rust-based backdoor as a background process, and the attacker also adds a cron job that repeats every 30 minutes for persistence.

The backdoor has been disguised as [kworker/u:8:0], while newer versions disguise the process as fc-cache and copy it to ~/.cache/fontconfig/fc-cache. Earlier samples used TLS/WebSockets for command-and-control communication, while newer versions disguise traffic as NTP by sending UDP packets to port 123 and using hostnames resembling time-syncing infrastructure. Until fixes are available, Sansec recommends disabling GraphQL and watching for unexpected Magento “Payment Transaction Failed Reminder” emails, suspicious processes, cron entries, and temporary files.

  • Fully updated Magento and Adobe Commerce systems may still be exposed, because the first observed exploitation hit a target running the latest security updates.
  • A sudden increase in Magento “Payment Transaction Failed Reminder” emails is a practical early warning sign of possible exploitation.
  • The backdoor’s newer versions try to blend in with normal server activity by disguising themselves as fc-cache and making network traffic look like NTP time-sync traffic over UDP port 123.
  • The malware checks Linux’s TracerPid value and will install but not beacon when tracing is detected, which may make some analysis or monitoring efforts miss active infections.
  • Rotating Magento credentials is recommended if compromise is suspected, indicating that attackers may gain access requiring credential cleanup even though Sansec did not observe follow-on activity.

Attackers are abusing a newly discovered flaw called “StyleSmuggler” in Magento and Adobe Commerce, software used by more than 160,000 online stores, including many major websites. The attacks can secretly install a hidden program on Linux servers that can contact the attackers and receive instructions. This matters because even sites running the latest security updates have been hit, and Adobe had not yet released a fix at the time of the report.

Mathspace discloses data breach affecting over 1 million people

Mathspace says attackers exploited a vulnerability in its self-hosted Metabase reporting system to steal personal data belonging to 1,079,819 students, staff, and parents or guardians in Australia and New Zealand. The company says passwords, credentials, tokens, and academic records were not exposed, but affected users should watch for suspicious account activity and phishing attempts.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Mathspace disclosed that attackers stole personal information belonging to 1,079,819 students, school staff, and parents or guardians in Australia and New Zealand.
  • 02Mathspace said the attackers exploited a security vulnerability in its self-hosted Metabase internal reporting system to obtain administrator access without a legitimate login.
  • 03The attackers gained access to Mathspace systems on August 10, downloaded data from the Australian reporting database on August 27, and Mathspace confirmed the data theft on September 3, 2026.
  • 04Mathspace said no academic records, learning activities, results, assessment records, passwords, authentication tokens, SSO credentials, or API credentials were exposed.
  • 05The incident is part of a wider set of data theft attacks involving compromised Metabase instances at companies including Trezor’s provider ShipMonk, Framework, and Tally.

Mathspace disclosed that attackers stole data from more than 1 million students, school staff, parents, and guardians after breaching its Metabase internal reporting system. The company confirmed the data theft on September 3, 2026, after attackers first gained access on August 10 and downloaded data from its Australian reporting database on August 27. Mathspace said 1,079,819 people were affected, and only people in Australia and New Zealand were impacted.

Mathspace CTO Alvin Savoy said the attackers exploited a security vulnerability in the company’s self-hosted Metabase installation, which allowed them to obtain administrator access without a legitimate login. The company said no academic records, learning activities, results, assessment records, passwords, authentication tokens, SSO credentials, or API credentials were exposed. However, Mathspace warned affected students and school staff to watch for suspicious account activity, including account-detail changes and password-reset messages.

The article says the Mathspace breach is part of a wider set of incidents involving Metabase instances at multiple companies worldwide over the last month. BleepingComputer previously reported that threat actors exploited a critical Metabase SQL injection zero-day vulnerability to gain administrator access and steal data from customer instances. The article also says Framework, Tally, and Trezor’s shipping and logistics provider ShipMonk were among affected organizations, and that ShinyHunters added Metabase to its dark web leak site on August 11.

  • Even though Mathspace says the exposed data did not include records linking users to schools, it acknowledged that schools with identifiable email domains may still be possible to associate with affected accounts.
  • Mathspace warned affected users to watch for account-detail changes and password-reset messages despite saying passwords, authentication tokens, SSO credentials, and API credentials were not exposed.
  • The attackers had access to Mathspace systems for more than two weeks before downloading data from the Australian reporting database, according to the timeline provided by the company.
  • The Mathspace incident was not isolated, as Framework, Tally, and ShipMonk-related Trezor data exposure were also tied in the article to compromised Metabase instances.

Mathspace, an online maths learning platform, says attackers broke into an internal reporting system and downloaded personal information for 1,079,819 students, school staff, and parents or guardians in Australia and New Zealand. The company says passwords, login tokens, and academic records were not taken, but the stolen information could still be used to target people with suspicious account messages or password-reset attempts. The incident is part of a wider series of break-ins involving the same reporting software used by other companies.

N-able patches max severity N-central flaw amid ongoing attacks

N-able issued an emergency hotfix for a maximum-severity RCE flaw in its N-central RMM platform and urged on-premises customers to upgrade immediately. Although N-able has not confirmed exploitation, Huntress warned of possible zero-day activity and said systems patched only to the previous hotfix remain vulnerable.
KEY POINTS
  • 01N-able released N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 4 to address CVE-2026-86218, a maximum-severity remote code execution flaw in its N-central remote monitoring and management platform.
  • 02CVE-2026-86218 allows threat actors without privileges to execute malicious code on unpatched N-central instances exposed online in low-complexity attacks.
  • 03N-able said it has no confirmation that CVE-2026-86218 has been exploited in production environments, but urged on-premises N-central customers to upgrade immediately.

N-able released an emergency hotfix for a maximum-severity remote code execution flaw affecting its N-central remote monitoring and management platform. The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-86218, allows threat actors without privileges to execute malicious code on unpatched N-central instances exposed online in low-complexity attacks. N-able addressed the issue with N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 4 and urged on-premises customers to upgrade immediately.

N-able said it has no confirmation that CVE-2026-86218 has been exploited in production environments, but warned that unpatched systems remain at risk. Huntress flagged the flaw as a potential zero-day and said it could not determine whether this new CVE or two earlier high-severity N-central vulnerabilities were used in a compromised customer environment because logs had already rotated. Shadowserver Foundation tracks nearly 1,500 N-central servers exposed online, most located in the United States and Europe.

  • Customers who applied N-central 2026.3 Hotfix 3 over the weekend are still not fully protected, because Huntress warned that HF3 remains vulnerable to CVE-2026-86218 and HF4 must be applied immediately.
  • The exploitation picture remains unclear because logs on the compromised customer N-central server had already rotated, preventing Huntress from determining whether CVE-2026-86218 or the earlier CVE-2026-86206 and CVE-2026-86207 flaws were used.
  • The risk is amplified by exposure: Shadowserver tracks nearly 1,500 internet-facing N-central servers, mostly in the United States and Europe, despite the platform being used to centrally manage client networks and devices.
  • The article shows a recurring pattern for N-central security issues, noting that one year earlier N-able patched two N-central flaws that were exploited in the wild and that 880 servers remained vulnerable days later.

N-able released an emergency fix for a very serious flaw in its N-central platform, which IT departments and managed service providers use to manage customer networks and devices from one web console. On-premises N-central customers are affected and are being told to upgrade immediately, because unpatched systems exposed to the internet could let outsiders run harmful code or gain access. Security researchers have seen signs that related problems may already have been used against at least one customer, and nearly 1,500 N-central servers are visible online, mostly in the United States and Europe.

Trezor data breach impact now reaches 81,000 customers

The company says wallets and Trezor systems were not compromised, but affected customers face increased phishing and physical security risks.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Trezor said an August data breach at its shipping and logistics provider ShipMonk now affects 81,000 customers in total.
  • 02The newly identified affected group includes 67,000 U.S. customers who ordered between November 2019 and August 2021 and had their names, email addresses, phone numbers, shipping addresses, and order numbers exposed.

  • 05Breach notification emails seen by BleepingComputer said attackers exploited a vulnerability in the third-party analytics platform Metabase, and BleepingComputer reported that ShipMonk received extortion emails from the ShinyHunters extortion gang.

Trezor says an August data breach at its shipping and logistics provider, ShipMonk, now affects a total of 81,000 customers. The company had initially disclosed on August 13 that nearly 14,000 customers were affected, including customers whose full names, shipping addresses, email addresses, and phone numbers were accessed. Trezor later confirmed that another 67,000 U.S. customers who ordered between November 2019 and August 2021 had their full details exposed, including name, email, phone number, shipping address, and order number. Trezor said the breach did not affect its operations or services, its systems were not compromised, and all Trezor devices are secure.

Trezor said the expanded impact occurred because ShipMonk failed to delete exposed data from its systems as required by Trezor’s contract and data policy, despite written assurances that the data had been deleted. The company warned affected customers of an increased risk of phishing, scam emails, fraudulent calls or letters, and potential physical security risks. Breach notification emails seen by BleepingComputer said attackers exploited a vulnerability in the third-party analytics platform Metabase. BleepingComputer also reported that ShipMonk received extortion emails from the ShinyHunters extortion gang, and that other companies in the Metabase campaign include Tally and Framework.

  • The breach impact expanded by nearly five times because ShipMonk retained older customer data from 2019 to 2021 despite Trezor saying it had repeatedly received written assurances that the data was deleted.
  • The exposed information creates risks beyond online scams because Trezor specifically warned that leaked shipping details could potentially expose affected customers to physical security risks.
  • The incident shows a supply-chain data exposure for Trezor customers rather than a compromise of Trezor’s own systems or hardware wallets, since Trezor said its operations, services, systems, and devices were not affected.
  • The same Metabase-related campaign has affected multiple companies, including Tally, Framework, and ShipMonk, according to the article.

Trezor says a break-in at its shipping and logistics provider, ShipMonk, exposed personal order details for 81,000 customers, including names, email addresses, phone numbers, shipping addresses, and order numbers. The newly confirmed group includes 67,000 U.S. customers who ordered between November 2019 and August 2021, in addition to customers Trezor had already reported in several other countries. Trezor says its own systems and devices were not compromised, but the exposed information could be used for scam emails, fraudulent calls or letters, and could create physical safety risks for affected people.

BigBear Microsoft 365 phishing service bypassed MFA at 258 organizations

BigBear 2.0, an Evilginx2-based phishing-as-a-service platform, bypassed Microsoft 365 MFA at 258 organizations by stealing credentials and authenticated session cookies. CloudSEK found over 5,000 credential records and recommends password resets, session revocation, token refreshes, and phishing-resistant authentication such as FIDO2/WebAuthn.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CloudSEK says the BigBear 2.0 phishing-as-a-service framework was used to bypass multi-factor authentication at 258 organizations and steal more than 5,000 Microsoft 365 credential records.
  • 02Researchers gained administrator access to the BigBear control panel and found 42 VPS nodes configured to target Microsoft 365 in the observed operation.
  • 03The campaign uses an Evilginx2-based adversary-in-the-middle framework to intercept passwords and authenticated session cookies after victims complete the multi-factor authentication process.
  • 04CloudSEK reported that the panel exfiltrated 5,137 credential records, including 474 complete MFA-bypassed authentications, 1,032 plaintext passwords, and 4,148 session cookies, affecting 3,331 unique victim IPs across more than 40 countries.
  • 05CloudSEK found that BigBear uses custom JavaScript to interfere with FIDO2/WebAuthn authentication and geo-matched residential proxies for 69 countries to reduce suspicious signals during Microsoft authentication.

A phishing-as-a-service framework called BigBear 2.0 has been used to bypass multi-factor authentication at 258 organizations and steal more than 5,000 Microsoft 365 credentials. CloudSEK researchers gained administrator access to the control panel and found 42 VPS nodes configured to target Microsoft 365. While 461 organizations appeared in the broader targeting dataset, CloudSEK clarified that 258 distinct organizations had at least one completed MFA-bypass compromise.

The campaign uses an Evilginx2-based adversary-in-the-middle framework to intercept passwords and authenticated session cookies after victims complete the multi-factor authentication process. BigBear uses a configuration called “offy” to set up a proxy between the victim and Microsoft’s legitimate authentication infrastructure, allowing attackers to capture credentials, MFA, and session cookies. CloudSEK said the panel exfiltrated 5,137 credential records, including 474 complete MFA-bypassed authentications, 1,032 plaintext passwords, and 4,148 session cookies, affecting 3,331 unique victim IPs across more than 40 countries.

CloudSEK also found that BigBear uses custom JavaScript to interfere with FIDO2/WebAuthn authentication and force targets toward weaker authentication methods. The platform uses geo-matched residential proxies for 69 countries to make activity appear less suspicious to Microsoft’s authentication servers. CloudSEK notified law enforcement and several affected organizations, and organizations potentially affected were advised to reset exposed passwords, revoke active sessions, refresh tokens, force re-authentication for high-privileged accounts, enforce phishing-resistant FIDO2/WebAuthn, and use Conditional Access policies requiring managed devices.

  • Geo-location checks alone are not reliable against this campaign because BigBear uses geo-matched residential proxies for 69 countries to make sign-ins appear to come from locations matching victims.
  • Organizations should not only reset exposed passwords but also revoke active sessions, refresh tokens, and force re-authentication because BigBear captures session cookies that can be replayed after login.
  • BigBear’s custom JavaScript specifically interferes with FIDO2/WebAuthn authentication to push targets toward weaker authentication methods, making strict enforcement of phishing-resistant authentication important.
  • The BigBear service appears to support multiple operators because CloudSEK identified at least five affiliate operators receiving stolen credentials in real time through Telegram exfiltration bots.
  • The administration panel remained online even though the phishing infrastructure had been offline for nearly three weeks, indicating that affected organizations still needed to treat exposed credentials and sessions as a live risk.

A service called BigBear 2.0 was used to trick people at 258 organizations into signing in to Microsoft 365, then steal their passwords and logged-in access even after they completed extra login checks. More than 5,000 records were stolen, which could let criminals read email, access files, and reach other work apps connected to the same account. This matters because Microsoft 365 is widely used for workplace email, Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, and sign-ins, so one stolen login session can expose a lot of business information.

OPEN SOURCE ↗

This is a specific, active phishing-as-a-service operation that bypassed Microsoft 365 MFA at 258 organizations and exposed thousands of credential records and session cookies. It is broadly relevant because Microsoft 365 is widely used and the article includes concrete defensive actions such as session revocation, token refreshes, and enforcing phishing-resistant authentication.

Hackers are exploiting a chain of two recently disclosed MikroTik RouterOS vulnerabilities to take control of routers with SSH services exposed to the internet. CVE-2026-67276 is an SSH authentication bypass caused by incomplete validation of RSA public keys, while CVE-2026-86060 is an SSH privilege escalation flaw involving specially crafted usernames. Poland’s CERT agency, which discovered the flaws with the help of GPT-5.5-cyber and GPT-5.6-sol, dubbed the exploit chain “MikroTrick” and warned that it is being actively exploited in the wild.

MikroTik fixed the vulnerabilities in RouterOS 7.25beta3, 7.24.2, 7.23.4, and 6.49.21, released on September 3, and Poland’s CERT validated the fixes. The updates add a compromise-detection mechanism that looks for known signs of unauthorized configuration changes at startup, disables malicious entries, and logs a critical warning, but CERT cautions that the absence of a compromise marker is not a guarantee that a router is clean. If compromise is suspected, CERT recommends isolating the router, preserving logs and configuration, factory-resetting the device, rebuilding it from a trusted configuration, and rotating passwords, keys, and other secrets.

  • MikroTik’s new compromise-detection mechanism can flag and disable known malicious configuration changes at startup, but Poland’s CERT warns that no warning marker does not prove the router is clean.

  • Poland’s CERT recommends rebuilding suspected compromised routers from a trusted configuration rather than simply cleaning individual settings, and also rotating passwords, keys, and other secrets.
  • The listed indicators of compromise include unusual SSH log entries involving user “-2,” a highly privileged “ops” account, and two IP addresses associated with confirmed or attempted MikroTrick activity.

Hackers are using two newly disclosed weaknesses in MikroTik router software to take full control of routers that have remote login exposed to the internet. People and organizations using affected MikroTik RouterOS versions are at risk, especially if those services are publicly reachable. This matters because routers help direct internet traffic, and a taken-over router can be changed by attackers; MikroTik has released fixes and Poland’s CERT says exposed services should be restricted if updates cannot be applied right away.

Security firm TantoSec published a working exploit chain for Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on a vulnerable server. Progress Software patched the flaws in version 2026.2.708 on July 8 and published the CVEs and advisory on July 22. The public release includes a detailed write-up, a command-line tool called telerik-rau-exploit, and two mixed-mode DLL payloads.

The chain affects the RadAsyncUpload file-upload control in versions 2010.1.309 through 2026.2.519, but running an affected version is not enough by itself. The application must render a RadAsyncUpload control whose server-side handler reads the upload result, and it must use an explicit non-default encryption key for the control. The article states there are no confirmed reports of exploitation in the wild, and the flaws were not in CISA’s Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog as of September 7.

The attack begins with a padding oracle in AES-CBC encrypted client-side state, where server responses reveal whether tampered data has valid padding or fails JSON parsing. This allows an attacker to decrypt and forge the upload configuration without knowing the key, then name an arbitrary .NET type that is resolved and deserialized into a gadget that loads an attacker-controlled DLL. Progress recommends upgrading to Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX 2026.2.708 or later and notes that successful exploitation may leave no obvious trace in standard ASP.NET error logs.

  • A custom encryption key, which Telerik recommends as hardening, is part of the required vulnerable configuration, and Progress warns that using a stronger custom key does not help because the oracle does not need to know the key.
  • The exploit is practical but noisy and slow, with TantoSec’s lab run requiring about 127,000 oracle requests and roughly an hour, making rate limiting and timing behavior relevant to defenders.
  • Hiding detailed error messages does not eliminate the issue, but it can force attackers onto the slower timing-based variant tracked as CVE-2026-13183.
  • Standard ASP.NET error logs may not show obvious evidence of successful exploitation, so Progress recommends looking for behavioral signs such as w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe, unexpected .aspx files, or mixed-mode DLLs in upload-related locations.
  • Sites that use affected Telerik UI versions are not automatically exploitable; applications without both the specific RadAsyncUpload usage pattern and explicit non-default encryption key are outside this particular chain.

A security firm published a working tool showing how attackers could take control of some websites using Telerik UI for ASP.NET AJAX, a software component used in web applications. Your Cloud Security Checklist Doesn't Work the Way You Think It Does

Intruder’s analysis of 3,000 cloud environments found that AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud fail in very different ways, so a single generic cloud security checklist is unlikely to address the biggest risks across providers. IAM and logging issues are nearly universal, while exposure, firewall, encryption, and service misconfiguration risks vary sharply by platform and organization size.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Intruder analyzed misconfiguration data from 3,000 organizations across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud for its 2026 Cloud Security Index.
  • 02Weak identity and access management controls and missing logging affected between 80% and 98% of accounts regardless of cloud provider.
  • 03AWS had the highest prevalence for exposed services, permissive firewalls, and weak encryption, while Google Cloud had the lowest prevalence in those categories.
  • 04Azure had the highest prevalence of misconfigured services at 80%, and its most common issues centered on storage account controls and Entra users without multi-factor authentication.
  • 05Weak IAM controls became more common as organizations grew, affecting 87% of SMEs, 95% of midmarket organizations, and 98% of large enterprises.

Intruder analyzed misconfiguration data from 3,000 organizations across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud for its 2026 Cloud Security Index. The article says risk profiles across the three providers have almost nothing in common, making it difficult for teams to rely on a single cloud security checklist. Weak identity and access management controls and missing logging were near-universal, affecting between 80% and 98% of accounts regardless of provider.

The largest provider-specific differences appeared in exposed services, permissive firewalls, weak encryption, and misconfigured services. AWS had the highest prevalence of exposed services at 76%, permissive firewalls at 83%, and weak encryption at 49%, while Google Cloud was lowest in those categories. Azure was the exception for misconfigured services, leading at 80%, and its most common issues centered on Storage Accounts and Entra users without multi-factor authentication.

Organization size also changed the risk picture, with most issue categories becoming less common as organizations grew. Weak IAM controls were the exception, affecting 87% of SMEs, 95% of midmarket organizations, and 98% of large enterprises. Midmarket organizations took the longest to remediate cloud issues, averaging 35 days, compared with 8–16 days for smaller businesses and 10 days for large enterprises.

  • A multi-cloud security program should not prioritize the same fixes equally across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud, because the article shows large provider-specific gaps such as exposed services affecting 76% of AWS accounts but only 8% of Google Cloud accounts.
  • Azure storage weaknesses tend to cluster together, since storage key rotation, access keys, and public network access issues affected similar shares of Azure accounts.
  • Improving network exposure and encryption controls may not address the most persistent risk in larger organizations, because weak IAM controls were the one category that became more prevalent as organization size increased.
  • Midmarket organizations may need special remediation support or prioritization, because they had the longest average cloud issue remediation time despite facing enterprise-level cloud complexity.
  • Google Cloud’s lower prevalence across most categories does not mean it is free from major security gaps, since its most common issues were concentrated around OS Login and service account controls.

Intruder studied cloud setup mistakes from 3,000 organizations using AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud and found that each provider tends to have different kinds of security gaps. Organizations of all sizes can be affected, especially those using more than one cloud service, because common problems include accounts with too much access, missing activity records, storage that is not fully locked down, and services exposed to the internet. This matters because one badly protected account or setting can give an attacker a way around other defenses, while teams with limited time may fix the wrong problems if they rely on a one-size-fits-all checklist.

Rogue ScreenConnect Clients Spread Four-Stage VBScript Chain to Newly Connected Hosts

Attackers are abusing rogue ConnectWise ScreenConnect clients to run a four-stage VBScript/PowerShell chain that can install backdoors, persistence tools, tunneling utilities, or an XMRig miner. Huntress says the activity has worm-like behavior because infected clients can push the same scripts to newly connected ScreenConnect hosts, and ConnectWise recommends disabling file transfers until a fix is available.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Huntress disclosed three unrelated August 2026 incidents in which attackers used different initial access methods to deploy rogue ConnectWise ScreenConnect clients that executed a four-stage VBScript chain.
  • 02The observed initial access methods were a Quick Assist tech-support scam, a phishing-delivered MSI installer, and a fake Geek Squad refund form lure.
  • 03The four scripts, named 1.vbs through 4.vbs, profile the host, retrieve staged data from Dropbox, select payloads based on host state values, and launch PowerShell to decrypt and run later-stage payloads.
  • 04Detected payload branches included a user-level ScreenConnect backdoor, tooling for UAC bypass and persistence, and tunneling utilities with an XMRig cryptocurrency miner.
  • 05ConnectWise said the issue affects file transfer behavior in both Cloud and On-Premise ScreenConnect deployments and advised customers to disable technicians’ file transfer permissions until a fix is available.

Cybersecurity researchers at Huntress disclosed worm-like activity that abuses ConnectWise ScreenConnect to distribute a malicious Visual Basic Script payload to newly connected systems. Three unrelated August 2026 incidents used different initial access methods: a Quick Assist tech-support scam, a phishing-delivered MSI installer, and a fake Geek Squad refund form lure. After rogue ScreenConnect clients were installed, they repeatedly spawned wscript.exe to run scripts named 1.vbs, 2.vbs, 3.vbs, and 4.vbs.

The four-stage chain profiles the host, records a state value in %TEMP%\value.txt, downloads staged content from Dropbox, selects payloads based on the recorded state, and uses PowerShell to decrypt and run later-stage content. Huntress detected different payload branches, including a user-level ScreenConnect backdoor, tooling for UAC bypass and persistence, and tunneling utilities with an XMRig cryptocurrency miner. In some cases, the scripts are written to C:\Users\Public\Libraries\Default\Lib\Lib1, enabling compromised hosts to deliver the malicious chain when a new Host connection is observed.

Huntress said the behavior effectively turns an infected ScreenConnect client into a content-delivery mechanism and can cause a server-side Host system to receive and execute the same four-stage script chain. The company recommended that affected hosts be re-imaged from known-good media or receive a clean operating system install. ConnectWise issued an advisory stating that the issue affects file transfer behavior in ScreenConnect Remote Access Support and Access sessions across Cloud and On-Premise deployments, and advised customers to disable technicians’ file transfer permissions until a fix is available.

  • The same VBScript chain appeared after three different lures, which means defenders cannot rely on a single initial access pattern to find this activity.
  • The infection logic uses host profiling results to choose different payloads, so two affected systems may show different follow-on behavior depending on installed security tools and existing ScreenConnect presence.
  • The activity can retrigger on later reconnections because the client records each ConnectionID only during the active session and removes it after disconnecting.
  • Huntress recommended re-imaging affected hosts from known-good media or performing a clean operating system install, indicating that normal cleanup may be insufficient for impacted machines.
  • ConnectWise’s interim mitigation is highly specific: remove TransferFiles or legacy TransferFilesInSession permissions from roles across every relevant session group.

Researchers found that criminals are misusing ConnectWise ScreenConnect, a tool meant for remote computer support, to spread harmful scripts onto computers that connect to an infected ScreenConnect client. People and organizations using ScreenConnect, including both cloud and self-hosted versions, can be affected because a new support connection may receive and run the same harmful files. The harmful chain can install hidden remote access, try to gain more control of the computer, set up tunnels, or run a cryptocurrency miner, so Huntress recommended rebuilding affected computers from clean media. ConnectWise told customers to reduce risk by turning off technicians’ ability to transfer files until a fix is available.

Check Point Research analyzed JSCeal, a compiled V8 JavaScript malware used in campaigns that redirect users from malicious Facebook and Google ads to fake cryptocurrency trading sites. The counterfeit sites tell users to download bogus TradingView installers, which lead to deployment of the malware. The activity overlaps with threat clusters tracked as WEEVILPROXY and MeadowLocust, and related campaigns have targeted retail traders and cryptocurrency investors across 12 countries in 25 languages, primarily in Asia Pacific and Latin America.

JSCeal is protected with javascript-obfuscator and uses techniques such as RC4-protected strings, control-flow flattening, proxy functions, and operation wrappers to complicate analysis. Check Point said it built a fully static deobfuscation pipeline to decode the compiled V8 JavaScript bytecode and recover details about the malware’s execution flow and capabilities. The malware can enumerate Chromium-based browsers including Chrome, Edge, Brave, Opera, Vivaldi, Avast Secure Browser, and Cốc Cốc, then extract cookies, saved passwords, OAuth tokens, and other browser data.

The malware can use stolen cookies to reconstruct browser sessions and carry out active session replay attacks that bypass authentication to access a victim’s Google account. It also includes surveillance functions such as keystroke recording and screenshots, along with proxy setup, certificate generation and installation, and service-specific request and response modification. Check Point found handlers focused on cryptocurrency platforms including Binance, Bybit, and Ledger, with some code capturing account data and cryptocurrency balances.

  • JSCeal’s operators combine compiled V8 bytecode with several layers of JavaScript obfuscation, which Check Point said moves the malware outside the workflows analysts normally rely on even though it does not make the malware impossible to reverse.
  • The SourTrade operation avoids sending finished malware over the network by having the victim’s browser retrieve a clean legitimate file and assemble the final malware in memory on the victim’s machine.
  • JSCeal’s local proxy capability is not limited to watching traffic, because the recovered code includes handlers that can modify selected requests and responses for Binance, Bybit, Ledger, and generic web content.
  • Check Point’s fully static deobfuscation pipeline shows that compiled and heavily obfuscated JavaScript malware can still be decoded without relying on dynamic execution.
  • The campaign’s continued activity into recent months and expanded platform coverage indicate that JSCeal remains under active development, according to the researchers.

Researchers analyzed JSCeal, a harmful program spread through fake cryptocurrency and trading websites that people reach from malicious ads on Facebook and Google. It mainly targets retail traders and cryptocurrency investors in 12 countries, especially in Asia Pacific and Latin America, by tricking them into downloading fake TradingView installers. The program can steal saved browser information such as passwords and sign-in cookies, record keystrokes, take screenshots, and use stolen Google session data to get into accounts without a normal login. This matters because victims’ online accounts and cryptocurrency services can be accessed or manipulated even when the fake site looks like a trusted brand.

  • The repeated hotfixes show continued pressure on the N-central 2026.3 line, with four hotfixes issued since August 2 across three distinct sets of vulnerabilities.

N-able issued an urgent fourth fix for its N-central remote monitoring product after a serious flaw was found that could let someone take control of an N-central server from the internet without logging in. This affects every customer running their own on-premises N-central server below version 2026.3.1.14, even those who installed the previous hotfix, while N-able says its hosted N-central service has already been patched. PEEP Turns Chrome and Edge Into Post-Compromise Backdoors for Host Command Execution

Researchers detailed PEEP, a post-compromise toolkit that turns Chrome and Edge into persistent backdoors by sideloading a fake bookmarks extension and using a native messaging host to run OS commands. It can steal browser data and cookies, hijack sessions, manage files, and maintain persistence by tampering with Chromium settings and policies.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cybersecurity researchers disclosed PEEP, a Chromium-based post-exploitation toolkit that masquerades as a bookmarks extension for Chrome and Edge.
  • 02PEEP requires prior administrative or code execution access and injects itself directly into Chrome or Edge profiles by forging Chromium Secure Preferences integrity values.
  • 03Once installed, PEEP polls its command-and-control server every 30 seconds over plaintext HTTP while exfiltrating browsing history, active-tab metadata, and session cookies.
  • 04PEEP uses a native-messaging tool called nm_host.exe to run host commands, manage files, and discover processes and services from the user context.

Cybersecurity researchers disclosed details of PEEP, a Chromium-based post-exploitation toolkit that masquerades as a bookmarks extension for Chrome and Edge. SOCRadar said the tool requires prior administrative or code execution access and injects the extension directly into browser profiles. It bypasses Web Store checks and user prompts by forging Chromium Secure Preferences integrity values.

Once installed, PEEP polls its command-and-control server every 30 seconds over plaintext HTTP for new commands. It exfiltrates browsing history, active-tab metadata, session cookies, and other automatically collected data such as public IP address, locale, and time zone. The extension also uses a native-messaging executable, nm_host.exe, to run shell commands, manage files, and discover processes and services.

PEEP builds on the open-source RedExt browser data analysis and red teaming framework and expands it with installation routines, a native host bridge, heartbeat telemetry, an update channel, and a broader command set. The article says the activity is unattributed, though Chinese-language artifacts in the source code point to a Chinese-speaking threat actor. SOCRadar said PEEP turns Chrome and Edge into persistent backdoors that can support credential theft, session abuse, and command execution.

  • PEEP’s use of Chromium Secure Preferences tampering is notable because it helps the fake extension remain auto-enabled even though it is not distributed through official browser extension marketplaces.
  • The native-messaging bridge is a major escalation point because it turns browser-level access into operating system-level command execution and file management.
  • PEEP’s reliance on plaintext HTTP for 30-second command polling creates observable network behavior tied to the listed command-and-control endpoints.
  • The presence of a Linux Secure Preferences patching script shows the operators were replicating the browser-persistence behavior beyond Windows environments.
  • The exposed “/health” endpoint reported 34 agent entries, 10 active sessions, and 507 data records, but the article says these cannot be confirmed as real infections rather than test entries.

Researchers found a tool called PEEP that can make Chrome and Edge secretly act like a back door on a computer after the attacker has already broken in some other way. It pretends to be a bookmarks add-on, then can collect browsing history, cookies, open page details, and run commands on the computer. People using infected Chrome or Edge browsers are affected, and the bigger risk is that a trusted browser can be turned into a hidden way to steal accounts, take over sessions, and control files.

DocuSign Lure With Zero Links and One Clickable Body

A DocuSign-themed phishing email evaded link detection by hiding its only external URL inside a full-card HTML image map instead of a normal anchor link. The message also spoofed the recipient’s own address with no SPF, DKIM, or DMARC authentication, making behavioral and sender anomaly detection the key signals.
KEY POINTS
  • 01A DocuSign-themed e-signature notice reached the chief executive of a small independent power and energy company with a branded document card and a named PDF that was only body text, not an attachment.
  • 02The incident record listed zero links and zero attachments, but the message contained a live external href inside an HTML image map area whose coordinates covered the entire visible card.
  • 03The destination was the root of done4you[.]tv, a domain with no visible connection to DocuSign or the recipient’s business, and the record contained no landing-page capture or scanner verdict for the host.
  • 04The From and To headers both used the recipient’s own mailbox, while SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and composite authentication all returned none.
  • 05The message was flagged by suspicious sender and behavioral signals, weighted by the recipient being a senior executive, and both occurrences were quarantined and permanently deleted.

A DocuSign-themed e-signature notice reached the chief executive of a small independent power and energy company. The message showed a branded document card with a headline offering disclosures for review and a named non-disclosure agreement PDF, but the PDF existed only as body text and there was no attachment. The structured incident record listed zero attachments and zero links, but the article explains that the zero-link result did not reflect the message’s actual click behavior.

The entire visible card was placed inside an HTML image map with one clickable area whose coordinates covered every rendered pixel. Its href pointed to the root of done4you[.]tv, an unrelated external domain with no visible connection to the e-signature brand or the recipient’s business. Because the message used no anchor tag and did not display the destination as visible text, an extractor focused on anchor elements and visible URL patterns returned an empty links array.

The From and To headers both contained the recipient’s own mailbox, and SPF, DKIM, DMARC, and composite authentication all returned none. The message was surfaced through suspicious sender and behavioral signals, with added weight from the mailbox belonging to a senior executive, rather than through URL analysis. The same lure reached the same mailbox twice, eleven days apart, and both occurrences were quarantined and permanently deleted after human review.

  • A “zero links” finding can be misleading when URL extraction only enumerates anchor tags, because an HTML image map area can still carry a clickable external href.
  • A message body that renders as one branded card should not be treated as clean solely because link extraction is empty, since the article shows the entire visible card can function as one hidden clickable region.
  • Self-addressed inbound mail from external infrastructure is a strong anomaly when no SPF, DKIM, DMARC, or composite authentication result supports the sender claim.
  • The slight subject change across two deliveries eleven days apart is treated in the article as a signal that the sender was testing whether the mailbox was live and whether the technique survived.
  • The article recommends extracting href attributes from image map area elements and image elements, not only from anchor elements, to close this detection gap.

A fake DocuSign email reached the chief executive of a small independent power and energy company and looked like a normal document notice, but clicking anywhere on the card would take the reader to an unrelated outside website. The email also pretended to come from the executive’s own mailbox, and the usual checks that prove who sent an email were all missing. This matters because tools that only look for ordinary links could say the message had no links at all, leaving a person more likely to trust and click a fake document notice.

StyleSmuggler is a new zero-day affecting every current version of Magento Open Source and Adobe Commerce, giving unauthenticated attackers remote code execution. Sansec reported that exploitation began on September 4, 2026, and the article says Adobe had not yet published an advisory, assigned a CVE, or released a patch or workaround. Aikido Intel rated the issue critical for Magento Open Source, Adobe Commerce, and the Magento Cloud metapackage.

The exploit works in two stages, starting with PHP injection through style properties in a GraphQL request. The payload is written into a Magento-generated file, such as a checkout failure report, and later executes when Magento renders a Payment Transaction Failed Reminder email. The email does not need to be delivered because the code runs server-side during template rendering.

Aikido Libraries released drop-in fixes for multiple affected branches that sanitize template styles before Magento’s engine processes them. The article says teams that cannot patch immediately can temporarily disable GraphQL, although this can take headless or PWA storefronts offline and does not fix the underlying flaw. Confirmed intrusions have installed a persistent Rust-based backdoor, putting customer personal information, payment transaction details, admin credentials, database contents, and shopper-facing skimmer injection risks at stake.

  • Disabling GraphQL is only an interim mitigation because it blocks the current entry point but does not fix the underlying flaw, and it can take headless or PWA storefronts offline.
  • The payload can execute even if the Payment Transaction Failed Reminder email is never delivered, because the code runs during server-side template rendering.
  • Being fully patched does not guarantee protection, since one confirmed victim was running 2.4.6-p15 with the July and August 2026 security patches applied.

The 72-Hour Reporting Obligation

The UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill’s 72-hour incident reporting requirement will be especially difficult for OT organisations because many lack current asset inventories, network diagrams, and operational documentation. The key takeaway is that credible reporting depends on pre-incident visibility, not scrambling to reconstruct OT environments after an attack.

  • 01The UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, as currently drafted, requires an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident and a fuller report within 72 hours.

  • 05The article argues that the 72-hour reporting obligation effectively tests whether an organisation had enough visibility into its environment before an incident occurred.

The article discusses the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill’s proposed two-stage incident reporting obligation. Organisations would need to issue an early warning within 24 hours of becoming aware of a significant incident, followed by a fuller report within 72 hours. Reports would have to be sent simultaneously to both the relevant sector regulator and the NCSC.

The article argues that the 72-hour window is much harder for OT organisations than for IT environments. A credible report needs pre-existing knowledge of which systems were affected, what those systems do operationally, what data or process capability they hold, the likely attack path, and the scope of exposure. The article says this information cannot be reliably reconstructed under pressure after an incident begins.

The article highlights a knowledge gap in many OT environments, where estates are built over decades, equipment is added without formal documentation, and network diagrams may not have been updated since commissioning. In some cases, knowledge about how systems connect and operate resides with individual engineers rather than written records. The article concludes that the 72-hour reporting obligation effectively tests whether an organisation had sufficient pre-incident visibility into its own environment.

  • The 72-hour deadline exposes a preparedness gap that exists before any incident begins, because the report depends on information that cannot reliably be created while systems are inaccessible and staff are responding under pressure.
  • OT organisations may be less constrained by the reporting timeline itself than by the absence of written, transferable knowledge about long-running environments that are often understood mainly by individual engineers.
  • The article frames regulatory reporting as a test of operational visibility rather than incident response performance, meaning compliance depends heavily on maintaining accurate asset, network, and process documentation in advance.
  • A report that looks credible to a regulator requires linking technical impact to operational function, not merely listing what was detected or shut down.

The article explains that the UK Cyber Security and Resilience Bill would require organisations to warn regulators and the NCSC within 24 hours of a serious incident, then send a fuller report within 72 hours. This is especially hard for organisations running operational technology, such as systems that support physical processes, because many do not have up-to-date records of what equipment they have, how it connects, or what it does. In the real world, that means they may be forced to explain what happened while systems are down, staff are busy handling the incident, and the information needed for a credible report may not exist in written form.

Emerging Threat: (CVE-2026-67281) MikroTik RouterOS Unauthenticated File Read via WebFig

MikroTik RouterOS has a high-severity unauthenticated WebFig file-read flaw, CVE-2026-67281, that can expose root-owned configuration files and credentials on unpatched devices. Organizations should update to the fixed RouterOS releases and restrict or disable WebFig access, especially on internet-facing routers.
KEY POINTS
  • 01CVE-2026-67281 is an unauthenticated file read vulnerability in WebFig, the web-based management interface in MikroTik RouterOS, with a CVSS v4.0 base score of 8.7.
  • 02The vulnerability can allow an attacker with network access to the WebFig interface to read root-owned files on the device, including configuration stores that hold credentials.
  • 03Affected RouterOS versions include 6.0.0 up to before 6.49.21, 7.0.0 up to before 7.23.4, and 7.24 up to before 7.24.2.
  • 04MikroTik has published fixed builds in RouterOS 6.49.21, 7.23.4, and 7.24.2, with a 7.25 beta build also carrying the fix.
  • 05The article recommends inventorying RouterOS devices, restricting or disabling WebFig access, blocking inbound TCP/80 and TCP/443 to router management addresses, rotating credentials after suspected exposure, and reviewing device logs for suspicious changes.

CVE-2026-67281 is an unauthenticated file read vulnerability in WebFig, the web-based management interface in MikroTik RouterOS. The flaw has a CVSS v4.0 base score of 8.7 and is mapped to CWE-824 and CWE-22. An attacker with network access to WebFig can manipulate the /jsproxy path behavior and use directory traversal inside an encrypted URI to read root-owned files, including configuration stores that hold credentials.

The affected versions span RouterOS 6.0.0 up to before 6.49.21, RouterOS 7.0.0 up to before 7.23.4, and RouterOS 7.24 up to before 7.24.2. Affected assets include MikroTik routers, switches, wireless access points, and Cloud Hosted Router instances with the www or www-ssl service reachable from an untrusted network. The article notes that these devices often sit at the network edge in branch, retail, small-office, VPN, aggregation, and cloud-hosted environments.

MikroTik has published fixed builds in RouterOS 6.49.21, 7.23.4, and 7.24.2, and a 7.25 beta build also carries the fix. The article says there is no public reporting of CVE-2026-67281 being exploited at the time of writing, while noting that CERT Polska reported in-the-wild exploitation involving the MikroTrick chain against the SSH service for the same release cluster. Recommended actions include inventorying RouterOS devices, restricting or disabling WebFig, blocking inbound TCP/80 and TCP/443 to router management addresses, rotating credentials after suspected exposure, and reviewing logs for unrecognized users, scripts, or scheduled tasks.

  • The article notes that there is no public reporting of CVE-2026-67281 being exploited yet, but warns that defenders should treat this only as a timing observation rather than a reason to deprioritize it.
  • The vendor advisory reportedly does not name CVE-2026-67281 or WebFig, so administrators relying only on MikroTik’s advisory may miss the specific version-to-vulnerability mapping described in the CVE record and third-party analysis.
  • A significant share of exposed assets were identified by service fingerprint rather than confirmed version detection, meaning the set of devices that need checking is broader than the set that can be externally confirmed as vulnerable.
  • Consumer Discretionary organizations represented 46.8% of observed assets, which the article links to distributed retail, apparel, and hospitality networks that often use inexpensive edge hardware managed outside central corporate configuration systems.
  • The article emphasizes that updating alone may not be enough, because MikroTik also directs administrators to inspect devices for flagged logs, unknown scripts, unfamiliar user accounts, or unexpected configuration entries after patching.

The article explains a newly disclosed problem in MikroTik RouterOS that can let someone reach the WebFig management page and read files from the device without logging in. It affects MikroTik routers, switches, wireless access points, and Cloud Hosted Router systems that have not been updated and have the web management service reachable from an untrusted network. This matters because those files can include saved credentials, and stolen credentials from a router can open the door to nearby management systems, VPN endpoints, and monitoring tools.
